IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management (target)

When Does Direct Collateral-Risk Certification Improve Slice-Aware Intrusion Response?

[Author names and affiliations to be supplied]
Preprint, 2 November 2026
Abstract—Mitigating a flagged user equipment harms benign users when the detector errs, and in a sliced 5G user plane the harm depends on the slice and the action. We ask when certifying each slice’s action-induced service-level-agreement (SLA) violation risk directly, using counterfactual replay and Learn-then-Test risk control, admits more attack mitigation than certifying per-slice false-positive rates. We prove that for a work-conserving water-filling scheduler, traffic-removing actions cannot harm non-acted users, so false-positive certification already bounds collateral. Relocating actions, such as redirection to a scrubbing service, break this bound. In a fluid simulator with a detector under domain shift, certified methods kept every budget in all splits. In eight pre-registered independent replications, the improvement of direct over false-positive certification was not confirmed: the mean change in delivered attack fraction was -0.030, with 95% interval [-0.071, +0.011]. With redirection, a post-hoc large-sample analysis showed the false-positive criterion accepting policies that exceed their budgets, although no finite-sample violations were observed; direct certification remained valid. The certificate should be chosen by action type.
Index Terms—Network slicing, intrusion response, risk control, Learn-then-Test, service-level agreements, false-positive control, user plane

1 Introduction

When an intrusion detector flags a user equipment (UE) in a sliced 5G network, the operator can rate-limit, block or redirect its traffic at the user-plane function (UPF). Each action harms benign users whenever the detector is wrong. How much harm depends on the action and on the slice: a blocked eMBB download degrades throughput, while a few slots of extra queueing break a URLLC deadline. Operators are accountable for this service-level harm, not for the false-alarm rate as such [1, 2].

Two lines of work address parts of the problem:

  • Calibrated detection. Finite-sample guarantees on false-positive or false-discovery rates [3], including recent detectors that calibrate alert thresholds by conformal risk control [4–6]. These certify an alert-level quantity.
  • Intrusion response. Optimised defensive actions, with guarantees that hold relative to an assumed attacker and system model [7–9].

Neither certifies, without a model, the fraction of benign users in each slice whose service-level agreement (SLA) is broken by the mitigation.

This paper studies one question:

For detector-triggered mitigation in a sliced user plane, when does certifying each slice’s action-induced SLA-violation risk directly admit more attack mitigation than certifying each slice’s false-positive rate, at equal per-slice budgets and confidence?

We do not claim to improve intrusion response in general. The comparison is between two ways of obtaining the same kind of guarantee.

The answer turns on a structural property of the user plane. If every action only removes traffic and the scheduler is a work-conserving weighted water-filling scheduler with per-slice buffers, then removing traffic never worsens the service of any other UE (Theorem 1). A per-slice false-positive certificate is then also a valid collateral certificate. Direct certification can gain only through the harm ratio between collateral and acted-benign fraction, and it pays for that with counterfactual replay and a larger hypothesis space. If an action relocates traffic, as redirection to a scrubbing service over the shared link does, the property fails, and the false-positive certificate can accept policies whose collateral exceeds the budget.

Contributions.

  1. Formulation and structure. We define per-slice action-induced collateral against the no-action counterfactual. We prove (Theorem 1, Appendix A) that the scheduler used in our evaluation is monotone, so collateral is bounded by the acted-benign fraction (Lemma 1). We also show by construction that relocating actions break this bound, including across slices.
  2. Certification procedure. RC-SIR applies Learn-then-Test (LTT) [10] over 1331 per-slice policies, with union-null p-values and fixed-sequence family-wise error control. The machinery is existing and used unchanged. We verify its implementation against known-risk Monte Carlo cases.
  3. Evidence, with pre-registered confirmation. An exploratory study, followed by a confirmatory analysis plan committed before data generation:
    • eight independent replications with randomised scenarios (Study C);
    • a non-monotone action study (Study N).
    Certified methods kept every budget in all 400 confirmatory splits. The pre-registered improvement claim of direct over FPR certification was not confirmed: the mean paired difference in delivered attack fraction was -0.030, with 95% interval [-0.071, +0.011], and 6 of 8 replications favoured direct certification. Under relocating actions, a post-hoc large-sample analysis shows the FPR criterion accepting policies whose collateral exceeds the budget. No finite-sample violation was observed (pre-registered hypothesis N-H2 not supported), and direct certification stayed valid.

All evidence comes from a fluid simulator. Section 8 states what this does not establish.

2 Related Work

Validity of ML-based intrusion detection.

  • Evaluation pitfalls and the operational cost of errors are well documented [1, 2].
  • Benchmark datasets contain design and labelling flaws [11, 12].
  • Detectors degrade across domains [13].
  • 5G datasets report near-perfect detection [14–16], whereas adversarial evaluation of 5G-core detectors shows fragility [17].

Calibrated detection.

  • Conformal p-values give exact FDR control for outlier detection [3].
  • TRANSCENDENT uses conformal evaluation to reject drifting samples [18].
  • FIRCE couples conformal evaluators with retraining [5].
  • CALIBURN sets streaming alert thresholds by regime-dependent conformal risk control [4].
  • An online conformal detector controls a smoothed FDR [6].

These methods certify detector outputs. Our per-slice FPR baseline is their slice-stratified analogue.

Risk control.

  • Conformal risk control (CRC) bounds monotone losses [19].
  • LTT handles non-monotone and multiple risks by multiple testing [10].
  • Weighted and adaptive variants address shift [20–22].
  • Conformal policy control regulates deviations from a safe policy [23].
  • Prediction-powered risk control reduces conservativeness using unlabelled data [24].

Response and mitigation.

  • Optimal-stopping and game-theoretic methods derive threshold response policies under a model [7–9].
  • Switch-native systems mitigate volumetric attacks at line rate [25].

Slicing.

  • RAN slicing with performance isolation [26].
  • Overbooking [27] and SLA-cost-aware forecasting [28] show that slices share and borrow capacity.
  • Network digital twins [29] are candidate replay engines.
  • Attacks on learned slicing controllers produce slice-dependent SLA violations [30].

Definition 1 (action-induced collateral).

Problem. Let be the expected fraction of attack traffic delivered in episodes that contain attackers. The goal is with the selected satisfying all constraints with probability at least over the calibration data.

Assumptions.

  • A1: calibration and deployment episodes are i.i.d.
  • A2: can be evaluated for every by replaying calibration episodes.

Theorem 1 (monotonicity of the scheduler). Suppose every action only reduces the traffic of the acted UE pointwise in time (as and do). Then, for every benign UE that is not acted on, the per-slot drop fraction and queueing delay of its slice do not increase. Hence .

The proof is in Appendix A. It uses the closed form of the allocation, a queue-comparison induction, and the inequality for overflow .

Lemma 1. Under the conditions of Theorem 1,

Proof. By Theorem 1, non-acted benign UEs contribute zero, and each acted UE contributes at most . ∎

Remark 1. Write , with and harm ratio . A per-slice FPR certificate requires ; direct certification requires only . A gain is possible only where and the threshold grid, after statistical margins, contains points between the two conditions.

Proposition 0 (relocation breaks Lemma 1). If an action relocates traffic onto shared resources rather than removing it, need not bound , even for slices in which no UE is acted on.

Proof (by construction). Take two eMBB UEs offering 30 and 26 units/slot and a URLLC UE offering 40 units/slot on a link with and shares . Without action, all SLAs hold. Redirecting the first eMBB UE to a borrow-only scrubbing class whose benign output re-enters eMBB one slot later raises the offered load to 126. The URLLC UE, which is not acted on and lies in another slice, then violates its SLA. Its slice has but . This case is a unit test in the released code. ∎

4 Certification Procedure

For calibration episodes , replay yields and for all . Let be the empirical mean collateral. Each is tested against the union null with where is the Hoeffding–Bentkus p-value for -bounded losses [10]. Family-wise error is controlled at in one of two ways:

  • Bonferroni (RC-SIR): threshold .
  • Fixed sequence (RC-SIR-FS): policies are ordered on half of the calibration set by and tested in that order on the other half, stopping at the first non-rejection.

The deployed policy minimises empirical over the certified set, with as a tie-breaker, where is the weighted benign-violation rate. The fallback is . Algorithm 1 gives the steps.

Algorithm 1. RC-SIR / RC-SIR-FS certification and selection
Input: calibration episodes e1..n; policy set Λ; budgets αs; level δ.
1. Replay every ei under all λ ∈ Λ and π0; record Lcs(ei;λ) and La(ei;λ).
2. Bonferroni: pλ = maxs pHB(R̂s(λ); αs, n); certify {λ : pλ ≤ δ/|Λ|}.
2’. Fixed sequence: split into halves D1, D2; order Λ by maxs R̂s(D1)(λ)/αs; test in order on D2 at level δ, stop at the first non-rejection.
3. Return argminλ∈Λ̂ R̂a(λ), or π0 if Λ̂ is empty.

Fig. 2 contrasts the procedure with the Slice-FPR baseline, which needs only benign scores and no replay.

Fig. 2. Certification workflow of RC-SIR-FS (steps 1–6) and the Slice-FPR baseline. Only the direct procedure requires counterfactual replay of every policy; only its guarantee holds without monotonicity.

Proposition 1 (validity). Under A1–A2, both variants satisfy . No monotonicity is required.

Proof. is valid for , because it dominates the valid p-value of a violating slice. Bonferroni, and fixed-sequence testing with an ordering independent of the testing half, control the family-wise error. On the complement of a family-wise error, every certified policy is feasible, so selection among them preserves the guarantee. has zero collateral. ∎

This is a direct consequence of LTT.

Corollary 1 (Slice-FPR certificate). Testing from the most conservative threshold downwards at level per slice certifies the per-slice FPR. Under Theorem 1 it certifies collateral. Under relocating actions it does not (Proposition 0).

Implementation verification.

  • Known-risk Monte Carlo. The certified variants were tested on synthetic loss tables with known risks and an adversarial selection objective that rewards risky policies. Over 1500 calibration draws, the selected policy violated a budget in 0.07% of draws for both variants (). Uncertified constrained selection did so in 100% of draws.
  • Consistency. A standalone reimplementation reproduces all published exploratory numbers exactly.

Complexity. Certification costs operations. Replay dominates: policy evaluations per calibration episode.

5 Experimental Design

Simulator.

  • Three slices, units/slot, shares , buffers , and 14/10/16 benign UEs per slice in the base scenario.
  • Observation and action windows of 30 and 120 slots.
  • Up to four attackers per episode: floods, pulsing floods and low-and-slow sources.
  • Rate-limit caps units/slot.

Detector shift. The detector is trained on a benchmark regime and deployed in an operational regime with:

  • additional benign behaviours (variable heavy users, URLLC alarm bursts, mMTC firmware bursts);
  • attackers that mimic their slice’s packet size in 70% of cases;
  • an unseen low-and-slow class.

This models cross-domain degradation [13]. The detector is an Isolation Forest [31] trained on benign benchmark-regime UEs; its score is the benign-training quantile. Thresholds are . Implementation uses scikit-learn [32].

Fig. 3 shows the resulting detector. On the deployment pool, its within-slice discrimination ranges from near chance in eMBB, where heavy benign users resemble floods, to near perfect in mMTC. This heterogeneity is what makes per-slice certification relevant.

Fig. 3. Primary detector on the 1500-episode deployment pool of the exploratory study. Left: per-slice ROC curves (false-positive axis log-linear); dots mark the five grid thresholds pooled over slices. Right: score distributions of benign UEs per slice and of attackers (log density); dotted lines are the grid thresholds.

Fixed settings. , , calibration episodes.

Exploratory study (v1).

  • One pool of 1500 episodes, 200 calibration/test splits.
  • Sweeps over and budget scale.
  • Load-shift and twin experiments.
  • A second (supervised) detector.

During this study we made two design changes, both disclosed in Appendix B: we replaced a first simulator version, and we corrected the selection objective. We also chose the fixed-sequence variant after seeing results.

Fig. 4. Study design. The exploratory study preceded a committed analysis plan; Studies C and N used only seeds and data generated after that commit, with method, endpoints and decision rule frozen.

Confirmatory studies (Fig. 4). Their analysis plan was committed to the repository before any confirmatory data existed, and was not modified.

Study C (eight independent replications, new seeds):

  • Each replication draws its scenario: UE counts ×U(0.75,1.25), attack probability U(0.4,0.8), perturbed shares and buffers, load range, and attack-slice probabilities.
  • Each trains a new detector on 600 episodes and generates 1500 deployment episodes, analysed over 50 splits.
  • Primary endpoint: the mean paired difference in delivered attack fraction (RC-SIR-FS minus Slice-FPR), with inference across replications by a t-interval and an exact sign test.
  • Pre-registered decision rule: the improvement claim is supported only if the 95% upper bound is below zero and at least 7 of 8 replications favour RC-SIR-FS.
  • Validity: violation frequency with Clopper–Pearson intervals, plus “confident violations” whose one-sided 95% Hoeffding lower bound on the test risk exceeds the budget. The latter separates calibration failures from test-set sampling error.

Study N (non-monotone actions):

  • Actions are block or redirect, in the base scenario with a new seed.
  • Redirection sends traffic through a borrow-only scrubbing class (weight 0.20) that removes attack traffic. Benign traffic returns to its slice one slot later.
  • Hypotheses:
    • N-H1: Lemma 1 fails empirically;
    • N-H2: Slice-FPR with redirect violates its budgets in more than of splits;
    • N-H3: RC-SIR-FS remains valid.

Baselines. All are evaluated on identical replayed outcomes:

  • Slice-FPR: Corollary 1, the strongest certified alternative.
  • Pooled LTT: one shared .
  • ERM: empirical constrained selection without a margin.
  • Conformal FPR 1% and a fixed threshold: alert-level operating points (exploratory study only).
  • No action and the Oracle (which blocks exactly the attackers).

Model-based response policies [7] optimise a different criterion and are outside the scope of the comparison.

  • Validity. No certified method exceeded its budgets in 200 splits. ERM violated them in 10.0% of splits at (equal to ) and in 25.5% at (Fig. 6).

6.2 Confirmatory Study C (independent replications)

Validity (Fig. 7). Pooled over 400 splits, RC-SIR-FS, RC-SIR, Slice-FPR and Pooled LTT never exceeded a budget (95% Clopper–Pearson upper bound 0.009). ERM exceeded one in 0.003 of splits. No violation of any method was “confident”, i.e. distinguishable from test-set sampling error.

Fig. 7. Study C. Left: per replication, delivered attack fraction against realised collateral relative to its budget (worst slice); grey lines connect the three methods of one replication. Certified methods used under half of their budgets; ERM used more and mitigated more. Right: budget-violation frequency over 400 splits with 95% Clopper–Pearson intervals; the dashed line is .

Primary endpoint (not confirmed; Fig. 8). The mean paired difference in delivered attack fraction, RC-SIR-FS minus Slice-FPR, was -0.030, with 95% t-interval [-0.071, +0.011]. 6 of 8 replications favoured RC-SIR-FS (exact sign test ). The pre-registered criterion (upper bound below zero and at least 7 of 8 replications) was not met.

Fig. 8. Study C primary endpoint. Per replication: mean paired difference in delivered attack fraction (RC-SIR-FS minus Slice-FPR) over 50 splits, with the 2.5–97.5% range across splits. Right column: share of splits in which RC-SIR-FS was better. Bottom: mean over the eight replications with its 95% t-interval, which includes zero.

The effect was heterogeneous (Table 4):

  • one replication showed a large gain (-0.144);
  • four showed small gains;
  • two were slightly negative.

Secondary endpoints.

  • The Bonferroni variant was worse than Slice-FPR: +0.051, interval [+0.009, +0.092].
  • Uncertified ERM delivered less attack traffic than RC-SIR-FS: RC-SIR-FS minus ERM was +0.052, interval [+0.011, +0.093]. That is the price of the certificate in scenarios where the budgets are slack.

Heterogeneity (post hoc, exploratory). We counted the eMBB, URLLC and mMTC thresholds in each replication’s population at which the FPR test needs more margin than the collateral test. These are thresholds where the acted fraction exceeds while collateral stays below , or where the acted fraction exceeds while collateral stays below it. The count correlated with the gain (Fig. 9; Spearman , eight replications). The three replications without such thresholds showed no gain. This agrees with Remark 1 but was not pre-registered.

Fig. 9. Post hoc, exploratory: per-replication gain against the number of thresholds in the Remark 1 band (horizontal jitter added). Replications without such thresholds show no gain.

6.3 Confirmatory Study N (relocating actions)

N-H1 (supported; Fig. 10). Under redirection, collateral exceeded the acted-benign fraction in 1.0% of episode–policy–slice entries, by up to 0.93. Two examples:

  • Redirecting in eMBB at threshold 0.995 gave eMBB collateral 0.0272 against an acted fraction of 0.0146.
  • Redirecting in eMBB at 0.95 caused URLLC collateral of 0.0055, although no URLLC UE was acted on.

Fig. 10. Collateral against acted-benign fraction for every (policy, slice) pair, population values. Left: traffic-removing actions (exploratory pool); no pair lies above the bound (Lemma 1). Right: block/redirect (Study N); pairs above the bound include slices with harmed by redirection in other slices. Inset: zoom near the origin.

N-H2 (not supported). Slice-FPR with redirection violated its budgets in 0.000 of 200 splits (95% CI up to 0.018). The finite-sample margin of the FPR test kept it at conservative thresholds, where the excess collateral stayed below the budgets.

A post-hoc large-sample analysis (not pre-registered; Fig. 11) treats all 1500 episodes as the population:

  • Redirect study: 31 of the 441 policies that satisfy the per-slice FPR criterion have collateral above a budget, all of them involving redirection. The largest excess is 0.0044.
  • Monotone study: the corresponding count is 0, as Lemma 1 requires.

The FPR certificate is therefore invalid in principle under relocation. In this model the error was small enough to be masked by statistical slack.

N-H3 (supported). RC-SIR-FS violated in 0.000 of splits (CI up to 0.018). It also delivered less attack traffic (0.448) than Slice-FPR with redirection (0.533) or with blocking (0.546). This utility comparison is exploratory. ERM violated in 3.5% of splits.

Fig. 11. Study N. Left: each of the 1331 policies by its FPR criterion () and its true collateral (), population values (post hoc). The shaded region holds policies that the FPR criterion accepts but whose collateral exceeds a budget; all such policies include redirection. Right: finite-sample outcomes over 200 splits (pre-registered).

6.4 Cost

  • Certification and selection on 500 episodes took 4.6 ms.
  • Replay dominates: 0.122 ms per policy–episode evaluation in the fluid model on 4 vCPUs, i.e. about 0.16 s per calibration episode for 1331 policies.
  • Slice-FPR needs no replay. A packet-level twin or testbed replay would be far slower, which favours Slice-FPR whenever its utility is comparable.

7 Discussion

The evidence supports a narrower answer than our exploratory study suggested.

Under traffic-removing actions (rate-limiting, blocking) and a monotone scheduler:

  • Per-slice FPR certification is already a collateral certificate (Theorem 1).
  • Direct certification did not deliver a confirmed improvement across independent scenarios.
  • A gain appears only when the threshold grid contains points that the FPR test cannot certify but the collateral test can. In our replications this depended on the eMBB harm ratio and on how close the acted fraction was to the budget.
  • Since Slice-FPR needs only benign scores and no replay, it is the reasonable default in this regime.

When actions relocate traffic (redirection to a scrubbing service over shared links, hairpinning, rerouting), the FPR criterion loses its justification. In the large-sample limit it accepted policies whose collateral exceeded the budget, including harm to slices in which no UE was acted on. Direct certification needs no monotonicity and remained valid. In Study N it also delivered less attack traffic than either FPR-certified variant, but that comparison was exploratory.

The practical recommendation is therefore to decide by action type:

  • Traffic-removing actions: use per-slice FPR certification.
  • Traffic-relocating actions: use direct, replay-based certification, and expect to need a replay engine with known fidelity.

Cost of a guarantee. In scenarios with slack budgets, the uncertified empirical rule mitigated more and rarely violated. A guarantee costs attack mitigation, and that cost is visible in our data.

8 Limitations and Threats to Validity

Simulation only.

  • All evidence comes from a fluid model with synthetic traffic.
  • No 5G core, UPF or RAN was available to this study.
  • Public 5G intrusion datasets [14] lack slice labels and SLA outcomes, so they cannot provide .
  • The guarantees (Proposition 1) do not depend on the simulator; the utility comparisons and the size of the harm ratios do.
  • Theorem 1 is proven for the modelled scheduler only. Congestion control, active queue management on shared queues, application retries and enforcement delay are not modelled; each could break monotonicity or change the harm ratios.

Statistics.

  • Exploratory splits reuse one pool; confirmatory inference uses eight independent replications, which is a small number.
  • Zero observed violations are consistent with the guarantee but say nothing about its tightness: realised collateral was well below the budgets.

Not compared.

  • Model-based response policies [7, 8].
  • Adaptive attackers.
  • Temporal dependence between episodes.

Twin transfer. Proposition 2 in Appendix A gives a valid but, at our sample sizes, vacuous guarantee.

9 Conclusion

We compared two ways of certifying the collateral SLA harm of detector-triggered mitigation in a sliced user plane: certifying it directly from counterfactual replay, or certifying per-slice false-positive rates.

For the scheduler we model, a proof shows that traffic-removing actions cannot harm non-acted UEs. Per-slice false-positive certification is then a sufficient collateral certificate. Across eight pre-registered independent replications, direct certification did not improve attack mitigation by a confirmed margin, and its Bonferroni form was worse.

Relocating actions break the monotonicity argument: the false-positive criterion accepted policies with excess collateral, while direct certification remained valid.

The results argue for choosing the certificate by action type. They also identify what is still needed: monotonicity analysis for real UPF implementations, replay engines with bounded error, and slice-labelled traces with SLA outcomes.

Appendix B: Disclosed Deviations

  1. First simulator. It had a single traffic regime and yielded a detector with AUC 0.99999, which made every method trivially valid. It was replaced by the benchmark/operational regime model before method results were analysed, and archived.
  2. Selection objective. The first full exploratory analysis used as the selection objective, contrary to the pre-specified objective . This was corrected; the -objective results are archived.
  3. Recommended variant. RC-SIR-FS was chosen as the recommended variant after the exploratory results. The confirmatory studies were designed to test it on new data.
  4. Supervised detector. A gradient-boosting detector with saturated scores made all methods coincide. It is reported only in the repository.
